solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Excited to go and do the unfinished pattern on fabric

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up and agitated, so the letters get thrown into a new order
something unfinished is missing its end, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
the two words run together, with the final E lopped off

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled to set off and finish a half-done pattern on some cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is TO GO plus DO THE without its last letter; 'and' simply joins the two lots of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogtooth is a broken check weave, closely related to houndstooth, used on tweed and suiting cloth.

clue.text: Sad face, taking in storm on vacation

indicators.note: to take something in is to admit it inside, so one piece goes within another
a vacated building has been emptied out, so only the outside letters of the word remain

blocks.note: dial is slang for a face
the word with its insides cleared out

explanation.surface: A gloomy expression on someone whose holiday has been ruined by a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: DIAL is informal British slang for a person's face; it takes in the first and last letters of 'storm'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dismal describes gloomy, depressing or miserable feelings, a close synonym for being unhappy.

clue.text: Elderly fellow reported a swindle after a thousand is taken

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the words are heard rather than read
something taken is removed and carried off, so those letters leave the word

blocks.note: a fellow could be called Jerry, spelt here to suit the sound
a swindle is a trick, and it runs straight on from the name when spoken
K stands for a thousand, as in 10K

explanation.surface: An old man tells people about a con trick involving a thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'Jerry, a trick' sounds like GERIATRICK; take out the K for a thousand and GERIATRIC is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Geriatric describes old people and their medical care, so it is a synonym, often jokey, for aged.

clue.text: Put down iron after crease initially comes out of collar

indicators.note: one thing coming after another places it second in the line of letters
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used
whatever comes out of something is removed from it, leaving the rest behind

blocks.note: to collar a suspect is to cop them, i.e. arrest them
the first letter of the word
to iron clothes is to press them

explanation.surface: Laundry instructions: put the iron down once the crease has come out of a shirt collar.
explanation.walkthrough: Collar looks like part of a shirt, but it is the verb meaning to arrest, as a police officer does.
explanation.definitionFit: To put down a people is to subjugate them by force, which is what oppressing means.

clue.text: Place to drive from, with refusal to waste a minute

indicators.note: what is wasted is thrown away and lost, so that letter disappears

blocks.note: golfers drive off the tee
nay is an old word for no
taken as written, and removed

explanation.surface: A golfer at the tee refuses to lose even a minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' reads as the noun of time, but it is the adjective meaning tiny, the definition. NAY without its A is NY.
explanation.definitionFit: Minute, pronounced my-NEWT, means extremely small, and teeny is a childlike word for exactly that.

clue.text: Rat briefly cuts supply in plant

indicators.note: said briefly, a word is cut short, so its last letter goes
read as the adverb of supple, meaning bendily, so the letters flex into a new shape

blocks.note: a rat is a cad, a contemptible man, shortened
taken as written

explanation.surface: Vermin chewing through the supply lines inside a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun, but it is the adverb from supple, meaning in a bending way; 'plant' is the living kind, not a factory.
explanation.definitionFit: A cactus is a spiny succulent from dry regions, one example of a flowering desert plant.

clue.text: Letters dispatched in fliers

blocks.note: surface reading: correspondence sent out inside leaflets or flyers
setter's reading: fliers are aeroplanes, so this is post carried by plane

explanation.walkthrough: Fliers suggests printed handbills, but here it means aircraft; letters sent in aircraft are the post that goes by plane.
explanation.definitionFit: Post carried overseas by aeroplane rather than by ship or road is known by this name.

clue.text: Locate neckwear taken from University Challenge?

indicators.note: something taken from a whole is subtracted, leaving the remainder

blocks.note: a feather boa is worn round the neck
the Oxford–Cambridge rowing contest is a challenge between universities; the question mark flags it as an example

explanation.surface: Trying to find the tie a contestant wore on the TV quiz University Challenge.
explanation.walkthrough: University Challenge wants to be the TV quiz, but it describes the Boat Race, the annual Oxford v Cambridge rowing race on the Thames. Remove BOA from the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To trace something is to track it down and find where it is, the same as locating it.

clue.text: Chat about hospital being involved in small leak

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: c. for circa, meaning about
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs
sm. is an abbreviation for small
to ooze is to leak slowly

explanation.surface: Talk about a hospital that has been caught up in a minor leak of information.
explanation.walkthrough: The leak sounds like leaked news, but it is a slow seep; SM is a standard short form in sizes and dictionaries.
explanation.definitionFit: To schmooze is to chat in a friendly, ingratiating way, often to win favour, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Runners on less firm terrain here – fine, in spite of stumbling

definitions.text: Runners on less firm terrain here
definitions.note: the answer is an adjective or adverb, read here as naming a place

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it
a stumbling walker lurches out of step, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
taken as written

explanation.surface: A skier's advice: the ungroomed snow is fine for your skis, even if you stumble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In spite of' looks like one phrase, but 'in' does its own job; the runners are skis, and F goes into the jumbled SPITE OF.
explanation.definitionFit: Skiing off the groomed slopes means going onto loose, unprepared snow away from the marked runs.

clue.text: Returning ingredients, a chef drops bananas, needing bread

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the letters run backwards
bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

blocks.note: the ingredients of something are its parts
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook sending back produce, dropping some fruit, and in need of a loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: Bananas and bread both look like kitchen items; one is the signal to rearrange and the other is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread is slang for money, so someone needing it is short of funds, which is the meaning of the idiom.

clue.text: One taking notice in my school

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: an ace is the one in a pack of cards
a notice in a paper is an ad
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pupil paying attention in class at my school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking notice' reads as paying attention, but it splits: 'taking ... in' holds the advertisement inside the card.
explanation.definitionFit: An academy is a school, especially a secondary or specialist one; in Britain it is a state-funded independent school.

clue.text: Award state power over psychological drug

indicators.note: turning over flips something around, so the letters run back to front

blocks.note: the OBE is a British honour, the Order of the British Empire
Cal is short for California
P is the symbol for power in physics

explanation.surface: An honour given for government strength in the field of mind-altering medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: The honour, the US state and the physics letter are strung together and the whole string is flipped.
explanation.definitionFit: A placebo is an inactive pill that works only through the patient's belief, so its effect is in the mind.

clue.text: Nancy’s very cross and that’s wrong

blocks.note: Nancy is a city in France, and French for very is très
to cross a border is to pass over it

explanation.surface: A woman called Nancy is furious and knows it is not right.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy looks like a woman's name, but it is the French city in Lorraine, so its word for very is French.
explanation.definitionFit: A trespass is an old word for a sin or offence, as in the Lord's Prayer, so it is a noun for a misdeed.

clue.text: Sweet drink – price, oddly, is around tuppence

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another
oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, so the first, third and fifth letters are kept

blocks.note: ale is beer
tuppence is two pennies, each written p
letters one, three and five of the word

explanation.surface: A sugary drink whose price is curiously about two pence.
explanation.walkthrough: Tuppence is British slang for two pennies, 2p; each penny is a p, so the drink wraps round two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a sweet is a dessert course, and apple pie is a classic one.

clue.text: Shoot gangster, heading west in capital

indicators.note: in an across answer west is leftwards, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: to zap is to shoot, as with a ray gun
Al Capone is the crossword's standard gangster

explanation.surface: Someone guns down a mobster who is fleeing westward through a city.
explanation.walkthrough: The gunfire and the gangster are both flipped together to spell the city.
explanation.definitionFit: La Paz is the seat of government of Bolivia, which counts it as its administrative capital.

clue.text: Visionary caught one in here

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: to be here is to be present
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A seer has been captured and locked up in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here' looks like a place word, but it means in attendance, the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Being prescient means knowing about things before they happen, as a visionary with foresight does.

clue.text: Arresting Liberal Democrat, copper picked up investigation – there’s only one way out of it

definitions.text: there’s only one way out of it

indicators.note: to arrest someone is to hold them, so one piece is held inside another
in a down answer, picking something up lifts it, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a police investigation is a case
LD is the abbreviation for a Lib Dem, from the UK's Liberal Democrat party

explanation.surface: A police officer arrests a politician and takes up the inquiry, leaving him cornered.
explanation.walkthrough: The copper is a police officer on the surface, but here it is the metal; the politician is caught between it and the upturned inquiry.
explanation.definitionFit: A cul-de-sac is a dead-end street, so the only exit is back the way you came in.

clue.text: First one off to get a tan? Better take top off

indicators.note: with the first one off, the opening letter is removed

blocks.note: to sun yourself is to get a tan
to cap a story is to better it

explanation.surface: Someone sunbathing is advised to remove their hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like advice, you had better, but it is the verb meaning to outdo.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncap a bottle or pen is to remove its lid, so it is exactly taking the top off.

clue.text: Covering miles, a swallow comes up onto mate’s tail feathers

indicators.note: to cover something is to go round it, so one piece encloses another
in a down answer, coming up means reading from the bottom to the top
a tail is the very end, so only the last letter counts
placed onto something means added on next to it

blocks.note: to swallow is to gulp
M is the abbreviation for miles
taken as written
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A migrating swallow flies up to its partner after covering great distances.
explanation.walkthrough: The swallow is a bird on the surface, but here it is the verb, to gulp; flipped, it wraps round the miles and the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Plumage is the collective word for a bird's covering of feathers.

clue.text: Cooked: did prune in advance?

blocks.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before
to pare is to trim or prune

explanation.surface: A cook trimmed the dried fruit ahead of time.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a whimsical split: the word read as PRE-PARED means trimmed beforehand.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooked food is food that has been made ready to eat, so the two past participles match.

clue.text: Parody about flower company’s final omission

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is placed around another

blocks.note: to ape is to mimic or parody
the Po is a river, and a flower is something that flows
Co is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A spoof of a florist firm that forgot something at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' wants to be a bloom, but in crosswords it is often a river, something that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: Apocope is the linguistic term for dropping the last sound or letter of a word, as in 'photo' for 'photograph'.

clue.text: Straighten back of jacket? I would, certainly

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the word's final letter
I'd is the contraction of I would
yup is informal for yes, certainly

explanation.surface: Asked whether they would smooth down the back of a jacket, someone agrees keenly.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in I'd vanishes in the grid, as punctuation always does.
explanation.definitionFit: To straighten a room is to make it neat and orderly, which is what tidying up does.

clue.text: Rhubarb found in beet, upside-down, back-to-front

indicators.note: found in means located inside, so the letters sit within the words that follow
back to front means the order is turned around, so read right to left

blocks.note: the letters sit across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A garden puzzle: a stalk of rhubarb turns up in a beetroot bed, upside down and back to front.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhubarb looks like the vegetable, fitting the beet, but it is slang for a row; 'upside-down' is part of the letters, not an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhubarb is informal, originally American, slang for a noisy argument or row, so it matches a quarrel.

clue.text: Dagger’s not used ’til fight

indicators.note: what is not used is left out, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: a stiletto is a slim dagger
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A knife stays sheathed until a brawl breaks out.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters T, I, L come out of the middle of the dagger's name, closing up the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A set-to is an informal word for a brief, heated fight or argument.

clue.text: Hoping to relieve pressure, cooked around 200 dumplings

indicators.note: to relieve someone of something is to take it away, so a letter goes
cooked means altered by heat and fiddled with, so the letters are reworked
around means surrounding, so one piece goes about another

blocks.note: taken as written
P is the physics symbol for pressure, removed
CC is 200 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A cook hoping to ease the strain has made two hundred dumplings.
explanation.walkthrough: Cooked sounds like the food being made, but it signals a rearrangement of the remaining letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnocchi are small Italian dumplings, usually of potato or semolina, so they are an example.

clue.text: Information needed by two guardian spirits

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information
II is two in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Two protective spirits need to be kept informed.
explanation.walkthrough: Gen is British army slang for information, as in 'get the gen'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Roman belief a genius was a guardian deity of a person or place, and genii is its plural.

clue.text: Once at my studio, I might produce such a programme

indicators.note: to produce is to make something new, so the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A television producer musing about what they might make once they reach their studio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Produce' sounds like television talk, fitting the studio, but it is the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A situation comedy, or sitcom, is a type of television series, so it is one kind of such show.

clue.text: Feline admirer not at ease in this?

indicators.note: not means without, so the following letters are removed

blocks.note: someone who admires cats
taken as written, removed

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a cat fancier might be uncomfortable in some setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At ease' looks like one phrase, but 'at' is the letters to remove and 'ease in this' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in clover is an idiom for living in comfort and luxury, so it is where one finds ease.

clue.text: Son that is returning gym skirt

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
id est is the Latin for 'that is', abbreviated i.e.
PE is physical education, school gym

explanation.surface: A boy is taking back his PE skirt to the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Skirt looks like clothing to go with the gym kit, but it is the verb meaning to go around; 'that is' is the Latin phrase written out in full.
explanation.definitionFit: To skirt a problem is to avoid it by going around it, and sidestepping is the same evasion.
